title: Organization of the Nervous System
think_prompt: How is the nervous system organized so that information can be processed centrally and carried throughout the body?
definition: The nervous system is organized into two main divisions: the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system.
description: This subunit introduces the overall organization of the nervous system. The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord, while the peripheral nervous system consists mainly of cranial nerves and spinal nerves.
key_points: Central nervous system|Peripheral nervous system|Brain|Spinal cord|Cranial nerves|Spinal nerves
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 science overview infographic showing a simplified human nervous system. Visually separate the brain and spinal cord as the Central Nervous System and the nerves extending throughout the body as the Peripheral Nervous System. Use a clear split layout or branching concept map, with minimal text and strong visual distinction between CNS and PNS. Clean textbook-quality educational style suitable for a classroom smart board.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify which structures appear central and which extend outward through the body.
quick_check: What are the two main divisions of the nervous system?
answer: The central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system.

title: Two Main Divisions — CNS and PNS
think_prompt: Why might the nervous system need one central part and another part extending throughout the body?
definition: The central nervous system includes the main coordinating centres, while the peripheral nervous system connects these centres with the rest of the body.
description: The nervous system can first be classified into the Central Nervous System (CNS) and Peripheral Nervous System (PNS). This broad division provides the framework for understanding the rest of the nervous system.
image_description: 16:9 split educational diagram. Left side: highlight only the brain and spinal cord and label the region CNS. Right side: highlight the nerves extending from the CNS to different body regions and label them PNS. Include one simple central branching title Nervous System → CNS / PNS. Avoid detailed brain anatomy and spinal-cord cross-sections.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to sort visible structures into CNS or PNS.
quick_check: Which division contains the brain and spinal cord?

title: Central Nervous System — Brain and Spinal Cord
think_prompt: Which two structures form the central part of the nervous system?
definition: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord.
description: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. They act as the central coordinating structures of the nervous system. Detailed structure and functions of these organs are studied in later subunits.
image_description: 16:9 clean anatomical overview showing only the brain and spinal cord within a human silhouette. Emphasize their continuity and central position. Label Brain and Spinal cord clearly, with a bracket or outline indicating Central Nervous System. Do not add cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla, grey matter, white matter, meninges or other later-unit details.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to name the two structures highlighted as the CNS.
quick_check: Name the two main parts of the central nervous system.
remarks: Keep detailed CNS anatomy for SU05 and SU06

title: Peripheral Nervous System
memory_badge: PNS links the CNS with the body
think_prompt: If the brain and spinal cord are central, how are they connected with distant parts of the body?
definition: The peripheral nervous system consists of nerves that connect the central nervous system with other parts of the body.
description: The peripheral nervous system extends beyond the brain and spinal cord. At this level, its main components are cranial nerves and spinal nerves.
key_points: Cranial nerves|Spinal nerves|Connections with CNS|Peripheral distribution
image_description: 16:9 human-body nervous-system illustration highlighting nerves extending away from the brain and spinal cord. Keep the brain and spinal cord visually subdued and emphasize the peripheral nerve network. Show two broad categories with simple callouts: cranial nerves emerging from the brain region and spinal nerves emerging from the spinal cord. Clean Grade 11 biology style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify where the peripheral nerves originate in relation to the CNS.
quick_check: What are the two main groups of nerves in the peripheral nervous system at this level?

title: Cranial Nerves — 12 Pairs
think_prompt: Which peripheral nerves are associated with the brain region?
definition: Cranial nerves are nerves of the peripheral nervous system associated with the brain, and there are 12 pairs.
description: Cranial nerves form one component of the peripheral nervous system. Grade 11 students should remember that humans have 12 pairs of cranial nerves. Detailed individual cranial-nerve names are outside this subunit.
image_description: 16:9 simplified educational diagram of the head and upper neck with the brain visible and several representative nerve pathways emerging from the brain region. Display a prominent but clean '12 pairs' memory cue. Do not attempt to draw or name all twelve cranial nerves individually. Focus on their association with the brain and their classification within the PNS.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to recall the number of cranial-nerve pairs and identify which major CNS organ they are associated with.
quick_check: How many pairs of cranial nerves are present in humans?
remarks: Number recall without overteaching cranial nerve anatomy

title: Spinal Nerves — 31 Pairs
think_prompt: Which peripheral nerves emerge in relation to the spinal cord?
definition: Spinal nerves are nerves of the peripheral nervous system associated with the spinal cord, and there are 31 pairs.
description: Spinal nerves form the other major component of the peripheral nervous system at this level. Humans have 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Their detailed roots and spinal-cord anatomy are studied later where relevant.
key_points: Spinal nerves|31 pairs|PNS|Associated with spinal cord
image_description: 16:9 simplified posterior or semi-transparent human-body diagram emphasizing the spinal cord and repeated pairs of peripheral nerves emerging along its length. Include a clear '31 pairs' memory cue. Avoid spinal-cord cross-section details, dorsal and ventral roots, grey matter or white matter. Keep the purpose classification-focused.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to compare the number and origin of spinal nerves with cranial nerves.
quick_check: How many pairs of spinal nerves are present in humans?
remarks: Number recall without entering SU06 anatomy

title: Overall Organization Map
memory_badge: See the whole system at once
think_prompt: Can you reconstruct the full organization of the nervous system from one starting point?
definition: The nervous system can be represented as a hierarchy of major divisions and their main components.
description: Organize the complete structure as: Nervous System → Central Nervous System and Peripheral Nervous System. CNS → Brain and Spinal cord. PNS → Cranial nerves (12 pairs) and Spinal nerves (31 pairs).
key_points: Nervous System|CNS → Brain + Spinal cord|PNS → Cranial nerves 12 pairs + Spinal nerves 31 pairs
image_description: 16:9 large hierarchical concept map for smart-board teaching. At the top show Nervous System. Branch into Central Nervous System and Peripheral Nervous System. Under CNS show Brain and Spinal cord. Under PNS show Cranial nerves — 12 pairs and Spinal nerves — 31 pairs. Use strong spacing, simple icons and large readable text. This should be the cleanest summary visual of the subunit.
interaction_instruction: Hide selected labels if possible during teaching and ask students to reconstruct the hierarchy aloud.
quick_check: Complete the hierarchy: PNS → ______ nerves and ______ nerves.

title: Classify the Structures
think_prompt: Can you place each structure in the correct division without looking back?
definition: Structures of the nervous system can be classified according to whether they belong to the CNS or PNS.
description: Classify the brain and spinal cord as CNS structures, and cranial nerves and spinal nerves as PNS structures. Recall the pair numbers for the two nerve groups.
key_points: Brain = CNS|Spinal cord = CNS|Cranial nerves = PNS, 12 pairs|Spinal nerves = PNS, 31 pairs
image_description: 16:9 retrieval-practice visual with four unlabeled or lettered items: brain, spinal cord, a cranial-nerve representation, and a spinal-nerve representation. Provide two empty category zones labelled CNS and PNS, plus small blank number boxes beside the two nerve items. Do not print the answers in the visual. Clean classroom assessment style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to place each item under CNS or PNS and supply 12 pairs or 31 pairs where appropriate.
quick_check: Classify these structures: brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves and spinal nerves.
answer: Brain and spinal cord belong to the CNS; cranial nerves and spinal nerves belong to the PNS.
remarks: Final retrieval check; detailed brain and spinal cord follow in later subunits
